'''David Jan Skorton''' is an American physician and academic. He has been president and chief executive officer of the [[Association of American Medical Colleges]] (AAMC) since July 15, 2019.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2018-12-20|title=Smithsonian Secretary Skorton to lead AAMC|url=https://www.modernhealthcare.com/article/20181220/NEWS/181229998/smithsonian-secretary-skorton-to-lead-aamc|access-date=2020-08-27|website=Modern Healthcare}}</ref> Prior to the AAMC, he led the [[Smithsonian Institution]], as its 13th Secretary from July 2015 to June 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2018-12-21|title=Smithsonian Secretary David Skorton Resigns After Raising $2 Billion for the Institution|url=https://hyperallergic.com/477335/smithsonian-secretary-david-skorton-resigns-after-raising-2-billion-for-the-institution/|access-date=2020-08-27|website=Hyperallergic}}</ref> A [[cardiologist]], he was president of [[Cornell University]] from 2006 to 2015.<ref>{{Cite news|last=O'Neal Parker|first=Lonnae|date=2014-03-10|title=Smithsonian Institution names Cornell president David J. Skorton as new leader|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/2014/03/10/cc7d2244-a85d-11e3-8d62-419db477a0e6_story.html|access-date=2020-08-27|newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Roig-Franzia|first=Manuel|date=2014-03-17|title=David Skorton, Cornell University's highly regarded president, is to lead the Smithsonian|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/david-skorton-cornell-universitys-highly-regarded-president-is-to-lead-the-smithsonian/2014/03/17/0f600340-ade7-11e3-a49e-76adc9210f19_story.html|access-date=2020-08-27|newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> Before arriving at Cornell, he served as president of the [[University of Iowa]], where he had been a longtime professor and then vice president. He began his career as a professor of medicine and engineering.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://newsdesk.si.edu/releases/smithsonian-regents-name-david-skorton-13th-smithsonian-secretary |title=Smithsonian Regents Name David Skorton 13th Smithsonian Secretary - Newsdesk|website=newsdesk.si.edu|access-date=June 14, 2017}}</ref> He was the first physician to serve as president of the Smithsonian Institution.

== Education ==
Skorton studied at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] before transferring to [[Northwestern University]], where he was awarded a bachelor's degree in [[psychology]] in 1970 and an [[Doctor of Medicine|M.D.]] in 1974.<ref name="oop">{{cite web|title=Office of the President: About the President|url=https://www.cornell.edu/president/about.cfm|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090707004518/http://www.cornell.edu/president/about.cfm|archive-date=July 7, 2009|access-date=July 9, 2009|publisher=Cornell University}}</ref> He completed his medical [[Residency (medicine)|residency]] and fellowship in [[cardiology]] at [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]], where he also served as chief medical resident.

== University of Iowa ==
Skorton began his career in [[Iowa]] in 1980, when he became an instructor at the [[University of Iowa]]. In 1981, he was named an assistant professor in internal medicine, and in 1982 he became an assistant professor in electrical and computer engineering.<ref name="Cornell Bio">{{cite web|url=https://www.cornell.edu/president/history_bio_skorton.cfm|title=David J. Skorton|work=Office of the President|publisher=[[Cornell University]]|access-date=March 15, 2011 |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110315075142/http://www.cornell.edu/president/history_bio_skorton.cfm|archive-date=March 15, 2011}}</ref> While at the University of Iowa, he also served as vice president for research and vice president for external relations. Skorton was selected to serve the state as the 19th president of the university.<ref name="Iowa President">{{cite web |url=http://www.uiowa.edu/~fyi/issues/issues2002_v40/01102003/skorton.html|title=The president among us: David J. Skorton named Iowa's 19th leader|date=January 10, 2003 |last=Schoon|first=Amy|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130503004335/http://www.uiowa.edu/~fyi/issues/issues2002_v40/01102003/skorton.html|archive-date=May 3, 2013}}</ref> He was appointed by the Board of Regents on January 5, 2003, and he served until 2006.

== Cornell University ==
[[File:Dr. David J. Skorton.jpg|thumb|Skorton's official portrait]]{{Multiple issues|{{Promotional|date=December 2019}}
{{BLP primary sources|date=December 2019}}|section=yes}}Skorton was named as the 12th president of [[Cornell University]] on January 21, 2006. He stayed at the University of Iowa for the duration of the 2006 spring semester and officially assumed the Cornell presidency on July 1, 2006.<ref name="oop"/> His inauguration occurred on September 7, 2006. In celebration of the occasion, the [[Cornell Dairy]] unveiled a new flavor of [[ice cream]], "Banana-Berry Skorton."<ref name="Barnes2006">{{cite news|url=http://cornellsun.com/node/18137|title=A 'Berry' Tasty Tradition: Ice Cream Named for Skorton |last=Barnes|first=Chris|date=September 7, 2006|publisher=[[The Cornell Daily Sun]]|access-date=July 9, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120223075621/http://cornellsun.com/node/18137|archive-date=February 23, 2012}}</ref> In 2014 Cornell announced that he would be departing to join the Smithsonian Institution, with his final day as president being June 30, 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2014/03/president-skorton-lead-smithsonian-institution|title=President David Skorton to lead Smithsonian Institution|date=March 10, 2014|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en|access-date=June 12, 2019}}</ref>

Skorton has been cited as one factor in increased donations to the university.<ref name="Frank2007">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/21/books/review/Frank-t.html?scp=23&sq=David%20Skorton&st=cse|title=Invisible Handcuffs |last=Frank|first=Robert|date=October 21, 2007|work=The New York Times |access-date=July 9, 2009}}</ref> During his tenure as president, Cornell's capital campaign raised over $4 billion in six years' time.<ref name="CampaignSite">{{citation|url=https://www.campaign.cornell.edu/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061030223604/http://campaign.cornell.edu/|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 30, 2006|title=The Campaign for Cornell}}</ref>

According to Cornell University, Skorton's base salary as president was $686,683 for 2009–2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.charitynavigator.org/index.cfm?bay=search.summary&orgid=3572|title=Cornell University|work=Charity Navigator |access-date=October 28, 2009}}</ref> Skorton held two academic positions while serving as president: a professor of pediatrics and internal medicine at [[Weill Cornell Medicine|Weill Cornell Medical College]] in New York City, and a professor of biomedical engineering at Cornell's College of Engineering on the Ithaca campus.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cardiologist, computer scientist, jazz musician: David J. Skorton named Cornell's 12th president |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2006/01/u-iowas-david-j-skorton-named-cornells-12th-president |access-date=2022-07-21 |website=Cornell Chronicle |language=en}}</ref>

=== Education reform ===
Skorton chaired the Business-Higher Education Forum and the Task Force on Diversifying the New York State Economy through Industry-Higher Education Partnerships.<ref name="oop"/> He established a University Diversity Council at Cornell University in 2006 and presently serves as its co-chair.<ref name="divcouncil">{{cite web |url=https://www.cornell.edu/diversity/offices/council.cfm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070529110809/http://www.cornell.edu/diversity/offices/council.cfm|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 29, 2007|title=Cornell's Commitment to Diversity: University Diversity Council |publisher=Cornell University|access-date=July 9, 2009}}</ref> He also writes monthly guest columns for the independent student newspaper, ''[[The Cornell Daily Sun]]'', a bi-monthly column for the Cornell Alumni Magazine, and blogs for Forbes.com and the Huffington Post.<ref name="oop"/> Skorton also spearheaded the Reimagining Cornell initiative.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cornell.edu/reimagining/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090704084243/http://www.cornell.edu/reimagining/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 4, 2009 |title=Cornell University: Reimagining Cornell : Home |publisher=Cornell.edu |access-date=December 27, 2010}}</ref>

=== Cornell NYC Tech ===
{{Main|Cornell NYC Tech}}
In 2011, Skorton led Cornell's effort to build a new applied sciences campus in New York City, in response to a competition designed by Mayor Michael Bloomberg to boost the city's technology startup sector. In partnership with the [[Technion - Israel Institute of Technology]], Cornell was selected as the competition's winner on December 19, 2011.<ref name=cornell1>{{cite web |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2011/12/cornell-wins-nyc-tech-campus-bid |title=Cornell wins NYC Tech Campus bid |publisher=Cornell Chronicle |date=December 19, 2011 |access-date=February 18, 2017}}</ref> In exchange for free land and $100 million for infrastructure upgrades, Cornell promised to invest over $2 billion in the new campus, called Cornell NYC Tech, over the next three decades.<ref name="cornell1"/>

Construction of the campus began in 2014 on the site of the Goldwater Hospital Campus on Roosevelt Island.<ref name="nytimes1">{{cite web|last=McGeehan |first=Patrick |url=http://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/05/21/cornells-high-tech-campus-will-have-a-temporary-home-at-google/ |title=Cornell's High-Tech Campus Will Have a Temporary Home at Google |work=The New York Times |date=May 21, 2012 |access-date=April 7, 2013}}</ref> On May 21, 2012, Skorton appeared at Google's New York headquarters to announce that the tech company would donate up to 58,000 square feet of space to house [[Cornell NYC Tech]] until the campus opened on Roosevelt Island in 2017.<ref name="nytimes1"/>

==== Immigration reform ====
Skorton was a proponent of [[immigration reform]], testifying on behalf of the [[Association of American Universities]] before the [[Senate Judiciary Committee]]'s Subcommittee on Immigration, Refugees, and Border Security in support of the [[DREAM Act]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://judiciary.senate.gov/about/subcommittees/immigration.cfm |title=Immigration, Refugees and Border Security |publisher=US Senate Committee on the Judiciary |access-date=April 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130403123546/http://www.judiciary.senate.gov/about/subcommittees/immigration.cfm |archive-date=April 3, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and specifically to allow more skilled immigrants to live and work in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|first=David J. |last=Skorton |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/david-j-skorton/immigration-reform-the-ec_b_914973.html |title=Immigration Reform: The Economic Argument |publisher=Huffington Post |date=August 1, 2011 |access-date=April 7, 2013}}</ref>

==== Higher education finances ====
Skorton argued that preserving college affordability must be a major priority of universities and Congress. Cornell substantially increased need-based financial aid under his tenure to off-set tuition increases.<ref>{{cite web |last=Otani |first=Akane |url=http://cornellsun.com/section/news/content/2011/11/17/university-spends-all-time-high-financial-aid |title=University Spends All-Time High on Financial Aid |publisher=The Cornell Daily Sun |date=November 17, 2011 |access-date=April 7, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130120035648/http://cornellsun.com/section/news/content/2011/11/17/university-spends-all-time-high-financial-aid |archive-date=January 20, 2013}}</ref>

==== Greek life and hazing ====
Skorton took national public positions on [[Hazing in Greek letter organizations|fraternity hazing]] and [[suicide prevention]]. Skorton pledged to end hazing in the [[Fraternities and sororities in North America|fraternity and sorority]] system, and wrote an op-ed on the topic in ''The New York Times''.<ref>{{cite news|last=Skorton|first=David J.|title=A Pledge to End Fraternity Hazing |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/24/opinion/a-pledge-to-end-fraternity-hazing.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=August 23, 2011}}</ref>

==== Suicide prevention ====
In 2010, Skorton responded to three student suicides<ref>{{cite news|last=Gabriel|first=Trip|title=After 3 Suspected Suicides, Cornell Reaches Out|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/03/17/education/17cornell.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=March 16, 2010}}</ref> by speaking out nationally for [[suicide prevention]], as well as authorizing the construction of barriers on the bridges over [[Cornell gorge suicides|Cornell's gorges]] and increasing resources for counseling on campus. Skorton also spoke out about the continued importance of the humanities to society.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/preventing-the-youngest-suicides/ |title=Preventing the Youngest Suicides |work=CBS News |date=October 3, 2010 |access-date=April 7, 2013}}</ref> The barriers were removed in favor of nets that were installed under each major bridge, a historically common place for suicides at Cornell.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://cornellsun.com/node/57060 |title=Three Years Later, Cornellians Celebrate Removal of Fences &#124; the Cornell Daily Sun |access-date=July 2, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130725160530/http://www.cornellsun.com/node/57060 |archive-date=July 25, 2013}}</ref>

==== Gun violence ====
Skorton joined eight other University presidents in signing a statement addressing gun violence in January 2013. The document called for the United States to "confront its culture of violence, particularly violence perpetrated by guns."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2013/01/skorton-signs-aau-statement-addressing-gun-violence |title=Skorton signs AAU statement addressing gun violence |publisher=Cornell Chronicle |date=January 3, 2013 |access-date=April 7, 2013}}</ref>

== Smithsonian Institution ==
Skorton became the 13th Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution on July 1, 2015.<ref name=":1" /> During his tenure the Smithsonian opened the [[National Museum of African American History and Culture]], its first new facility on the [[National Mall]] since the opening of the [[National Museum of the American Indian]] in 2004.{{Citation needed|date=November 2023}}

He was elected a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://amphilsoc.org/members/electedApril2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170915195158/https://amphilsoc.org/members/electedApril2017|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 15, 2017|title=Newly Elected - April 2017 - American Philosophical Society|date=September 15, 2017|access-date=December 20, 2018}}</ref>

In December 2018, the Smithsonian announced<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/20/arts/design/david-skorton-smithsonian.html|title=David J. Skorton Is Leaving the Smithsonian for a Health Care Nonprofit|last=Bowley|first=Graham|date=December 20, 2018|work=The New York Times|access-date=June 12, 2019|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> that Skorton would be leaving his position in June 2019 to become president and CEO of the Association of American Medical Colleges. [[Lonnie Bunch]], director of the African American History Museum, succeeded Skorton and became the 14th Secretary on June 16, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/06/12/730795443/lonnie-bunch-iii-takes-helm-of-the-smithsonian-i-feel-the-weight-of-history|title=Lonnie Bunch III Takes Helm Of The Smithsonian: 'I Feel The Weight Of History'|website=NPR.org|date=June 12, 2019 |language=en|access-date=June 12, 2019 |last1=Axelrod |first1=Josh }}</ref>

== Association of American Medical Colleges ==
David Skorton is president and CEO of the [[Association of American Medical Colleges]] (AAMC), a non-profit organization based in Washington, D.C.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Bohanon|first=Mariah|title=AAMC Head and DEI Advocate David Skorton Faces COVID-19 Crisis After Less Than a Year in Office|date=May 19, 2020 |url=https://www.insightintodiversity.com/aamc-head-and-dei-advocate-david-skorton-faces-covid-19-crisis-after-less-than-a-year-in-office/|access-date=2020-08-12|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Diversity, equity, and inclusion ===
When he assumed the presidency of the AAMC, Skorton said he would focus on three challenges: [[diversity, equity, and inclusion]] (DEI); mental health and substance use disorders; and access and affordability of care.<ref name=":0" />

In November 2019, he wrote an op-ed for ''[[The Washington Post]]'' that called for the Supreme Court to consider the negative effects that would result from deporting the approximately 27,000 healthcare workers with [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals|DACA]] status. This was just before the Supreme Court began its DACA hearings.<ref name=":0" /> In June 2020, when the Supreme Court ruled that DACA could not be ended, Skorton praised the decision, stating that the AAMC was appreciative that the ruling allowed those healthcare workers to continue providing care throughout the U.S.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What the Supreme Court's ruling on DACA means for health care|url=http://www.advisory.com/daily-briefing/2020/06/19/daca|access-date=2020-09-02|website=www.advisory.com}}</ref>

In January 2020, he issued a call to action to medical schools as the first step in an initiative to improve equity in pay, promotion, and other areas for women.<ref name=":0" /> In December 2019, the AAMC released data that showed that, for the first time in history, women comprise the majority of enrolled medical students in the U.S., at 50.5%.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Women Now the Majority of U.S. Medical Students, AAMC Data Reveals|url=https://diverseeducation.com/article/161905/|access-date=2020-10-14|website=Diverse|date=December 10, 2019 }}</ref>

In response to both the COVID-19 pandemic and the impact of structural racism on people in vulnerable communities, Skorton argued that there is a need for a national standardized system for the collection of race and ethnicity data related to the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-04-16|title=AAMC CEO says better testing needed if nation is to reopen|url=https://www.modernhealthcare.com/providers/qa-aamc-ceo-says-better-testing-needed-if-nation-reopen|website=Modern Healthcare}}</ref>

=== Coronavirus response ===
After less than a year in office, Skorton was responsible for leading the AAMC's 171 medical schools and over 400 teaching hospitals and systems through the initial phases of the coronavirus pandemic.<ref name=":0" /> Throughout 2020, the AAMC was criticized for continuing to hold the [[Medical College Admission Test|MCAT]] exam in person during the [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID pandemic.]]<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rabin |first=Roni Caryn |date=2020-08-07 |title=Want to Be a Doctor? Take Your Chances in a Closed Room With Strangers |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/08/07/health/coronavirus-exams-mcat.html |access-date=2023-11-03 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In July 2020, Skorton joined other executives at the AAMC in issuing a statement in support of [[Anthony Fauci|Dr. Anthony Fauci]], the top federal infectious disease official.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trump retweets game show host Chuck Woolery's baseless claim that 'everyone is lying' about coronavirus|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/07/13/coronavirus-trump-cites-chuck-woolery-questioning-covid-19-on-twitter.html|access-date=2020-08-24|website=CNBC|date=July 13, 2020|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-07-14|title=Medical Groups Back Fauci Against White House Criticism|url=https://www.medpagetoday.com/infectiousdisease/covid19/87557|access-date=2020-08-24|website=MedPageToday|language=en}}</ref> Later that month, Skorton oversaw the release of a proposed plan to reset the U.S.’s response to the pandemic. The plan consisted of nine immediate actions, such as increasing production of key supplies and establishing national criteria for stay-at-home orders; and two longer-term actions, including broadening health insurance.<ref>{{Cite web|title=An expert-backed roadmap to reset our pandemic response| website=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]] |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/expert-backed-roadmap-reset-pandemic-response/story?id=72077859}}</ref> In August 2020, Skorton released a statement that the AAMC was alarmed at changes to the CDC’s testing guidelines for individuals not showing symptoms of the disease.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Providers speak out against new testing guidelines|url=https://www.healthcarefinancenews.com/news/providers-speak-out-against-new-testing-guidelines|access-date=2020-10-14|website=Healthcare Finance News|language=en}}</ref>

==Other work==

In 2012, Skorton was appointed to the [[New York Racing Association]] Reorganizational Board, by then governor [[Andrew Cuomo]] along with 16 other public figures "putting in place a temporary, publicly controlled body to transform management of thoroughbred racing in New York State."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Admin |first=NYTB |date=2012-10-18 |title=Cornell President David Skorton to Chair NYRA Reorganization Board |url=https://www.nytbreeders.org/news/2012/10/18/nyra-reorganization-board-announcement/ |access-date=2026-10-08 |website=New York Thoroughbred Breeders, Inc. News |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2020, Skorton was named a volunteer member of the [[Presidential transition of Joe Biden|Joe Biden presidential transition]] Agency Review Team to support transition efforts related to the arts and humanities.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agency Review Teams |url=https://buildbackbetter.com/the-transition/agency-review-teams/ |website=President-Elect Joe Biden |access-date=10 November 2020 |archive-date=August 28, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220828180800/https://www.whitehouse.gov/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Skorton is an avid musician. He once worked as a professional jazz and R&B performer in the Chicago area. He began playing saxophone at age 9<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jazz and haiku: Skorton sees arts and humanities as university's 'soul'|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2006/01/jazz-and-haiku-skorton-sees-arts-and-humanities-universitys-soul|access-date=2020-11-25|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en}}</ref> and also plays the flute. He was also co-host of a weekly program, "As Night Falls - Latin Jazz," on KSUI FM, the University of Iowa's public radio station.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cardiologist, computer scientist, jazz musician: David J. Skorton named Cornell's 12th president|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2006/01/u-iowas-david-j-skorton-named-cornells-12th-president|access-date=2020-11-25|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en}}</ref>

== Honors ==
* In 2010, Skorton was elected as a member of the [[National Academy of Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=National Academy of Medicine|url=https://nam.edu/member/?member_id=%2F3j0gElY%2BgAKMNTGvsKBvg%3D%3D}}</ref>
* In 2011, Skorton was elected as a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|date=January 22, 2024 |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/david-j-skorton}}</ref>
* In 2015, Skorton was awarded the Arts and Sciences Advocacy Award from the [[Council of Colleges of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ccas.net/i4a/pages/index.cfm?pageid=3636|title=Arts & Sciences Advocacy Award - Council of Colleges of Arts and Sciences|website=www.ccas.net|access-date=May 2, 2016}}</ref>
* In 2017, Skorton was elected as a member of [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Skorton}}</ref>
* Skorton is also a member of the [[Council on Foreign Relations]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Council on Foreign Relations|url=https://www.cfr.org/membership/roster}}</ref> and a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Elected Fellows American Association for the Advancement of Science|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/listing}}</ref>
